claims.source: SPoC is a supervised regression approach, in which a target variable (here: subjective emotional arousal) guides the extraction of relevant M/EEG oscillatory components (here: alpha power).
claims.evidence: This describes the SPoC method used in the study.

claims.claim: SPoC has been used to predict single-trial reaction times from alpha power in a hand motor task.
claims.source: SPoC has been used to predict single-trial reaction times from alpha power in a hand motor task (Meinel et al., 2016), muscular contraction from beta power (Sabbagh et al., 2020), and difficulty levels of a video game from theta and alpha power (Naumann et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Meinel et al., 2016.

claims.claim: CSP is used to decompose a multivariate signal into components that maximize the difference in variance between distinct classes.
claims.source: CSP is used to decompose a multivariate signal into components that maximize the difference in variance between distinct classes (here: periods of high and low emotional arousal).
claims.evidence: This describes the CSP method used in the study.

claims.claim: CSP is being used with EEG for brain-computer interfaces.
claims.source: CSP is being used with EEG for BCI (Blankertz et al., 2008) or to decode workload (Schultze-Kraft et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Blankertz et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Long short-term memory recurrent neural networks are particularly suited for time-sequential data.
claims.source: For time-sequential data, long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are particularly suited (Greff et al., 2017; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1995; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Greff et al., 2017, Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1995, and Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997.

claims.claim: LSTMs have been successfully applied for speech recognition, language translation, and scene analysis in videos.
claims.source: LSTMs have been successfully applied for speech recognition (Graves et al., 2013), language translation (Luong et al., 2015), or scene analysis in videos (Donahue et al., 2015), but also to detect emotions in speech and facial expressions (Wöllmer et al., 2010; Wöllmer et al., 2008) or workload in EEG (Bashivan et al., 2016; Hefron et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Graves et al., 2013, Luong et al., 2015, and Donahue et al., 2015.

claims.claim: LSTMs have been applied to detect emotions in speech and facial expressions.
claims.source: LSTMs have been successfully applied for speech recognition (Graves et al., 2013), language translation (Luong et al., 2015), or scene analysis in videos (Donahue et al., 2015), but also to detect emotions in speech and facial expressions (Wöllmer et al., 2010; Wöllmer et al., 2008) or workload in EEG (Bashivan et al., 2016; Hefron et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wöllmer et al., 2010 and Wöllmer et al., 2008.

claims.claim: LSTMs have been applied to decode workload in EEG.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bashivan et al., 2016 and Hefron et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Forty-five healthy young participants were recruited for the study.
claims.source: Forty-five healthy young participants were recruited via the participant database at the Berlin School of Mind and Brain (an adaption of ORSEE; Greiner, 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the study.

claims.claim: Previous studies on the relationship between emotional arousal and neural oscillations reported samples of 19–32 subjects.
claims.source: Previous studies on the relationship between emotional arousal and neural oscillations reported samples of 19–32 subjects (e.g., Koelstra et al., 2012; Luft and Bhattacharya, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Koelstra et al., 2012 and Luft and Bhattacharya, 2015.

claims.claim: Thirty channels of EEG activity were recorded in accordance with the international 10/20 system.
claims.source: Thirty channels of EEG activity were recorded in accordance with the international 10/20 system (Sharbrough et al., 1991) using a mobile amplifier (LiveAmp32) and active electrodes (actiCap; both by BrainProducts, Gilching, Germany, RRID:SCR_009443).
claims.evidence: This describes the EEG recording setup.

claims.claim: Data were sampled at 500 Hz with a hardware-based low-pass filter at 131 Hz.
claims.source: Data were sampled at 500 Hz with a hardware-based low-pass filter at 131 Hz and referenced to electrode FCz.
claims.evidence: This describes the EEG data acquisition parameters.

claims.claim: An HTC Vive head-mounted display was used for the VR experience.
claims.source: An HTC Vive head-mounted display (HMD; HTC, New Taipei, Taiwan) and headphones (AIAIAI Tracks, ApS, Copenhagen, Denmark) were placed on top of the EEG cap using small, custom-made cushions to avoid pressure artefacts and increase comfort.
claims.evidence: This describes the VR equipment used in the study.

claims.claim: The HTC Vive provides stereoscopy with two 1080 × 1200-pixel OLED displays, a 110° field-of-view, and a frame rate of 90 Hz.
claims.source: The HTC Vive provides stereoscopy with two 1080 × 1200-pixel OLED displays, a 110° field-of-view, and a frame rate of 90 Hz.
claims.evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the VR headset.

claims.claim: Stimulation comprised two commercially available rollercoaster rides separated by a 30 s break.
claims.source: Stimulation comprised two commercially available rollercoaster rides ('Russian VR Coasters' by Funny Twins Games, Ekaterinburg, Russia, on Steam) that were separated by a 30 s break (during which participants kept their eyes open and looked straight): the 'Space' rollercoaster, a 153 s ride through planets, asteroids, and spaceships and the 'Andes' rollercoaster, a 97 s ride through a mountain scenery (for more details, see Figure 5 and the Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the VR stimulation used in the study.

claims.claim: The 'Space' rollercoaster was a 153 s ride through planets, asteroids, and spaceships.
claims.source: the 'Space' rollercoaster, a 153 s ride through planets, asteroids, and spaceships and the 'Andes' rollercoaster, a 97 s ride through a mountain scenery (for more details, see Figure 5 and the Appendix 1).

claims.claim: The 'Andes' rollercoaster was a 97 s ride through a mountain scenery.

claims.claim: After each VR experience, participants watched a 2D recording of their experience and continuously rated their emotional arousal by turning a dial.
claims.source: After each VR experience, participants watched a 2D recording (recorded using OBS Studio, https://obsproject.com/) of their experience on a virtual screen (SteamVR's 'view desktop' feature), that is, without removing the HMD. They recalled and continuously rated their emotional arousal by turning a dial (PowerMate USB, Griffin Technology, Corona, CA; sampling frequency: 50 Hz), with which they manipulated a vertical rating bar, displayed next to the video, ranging from low (0) to high (100) in 50 discrete steps (McCall et al., 2015; see Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the rating procedure.

claims.claim: Each participant completed the VR episode twice: once while not moving the head and once while freely moving the head.
claims.source: Importantly, each participant completed the VR episode (plus rating) twice: once while not moving the head (nomov condition) and once while freely moving the head (mov condition) during the VR experience.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claims.claim: The sequence of the movement conditions was counterbalanced across participants.
claims.source: The sequence of the movement conditions was counterbalanced across participants (n = 19 with nomov condition first).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for order effects.

claims.claim: Data from eight participants needed to be discarded due to technical problems or electrode malfunctioning.
claims.source: Data from eight participants needed to be discarded due to technical problems (n = 5) or electrode malfunctioning (n = 1); one participant discontinued the experiment and another participant reported having taken psychoactive medication.
claims.evidence: This describes data exclusions.

claims.claim: The data from 37 participants entered the analysis.
claims.source: The data from 37 participants entered the analysis (17 men, age: M ± SD: 25.1 ± 3.1, range: 20–31 years).

claims.claim: After quality assurance during the EEG preprocessing, data from 26 participants in the condition with no head movement and 19 in condition with free head movement entered the statistical analyses that included EEG data.
claims.source: After quality assurance during the EEG preprocessing, data from 26 participants in the condition with no head movement (nomov) and 19 in condition with free head movement (mov) entered the statistical analyses that included EEG data.
claims.evidence: This describes the final sample sizes per condition after preprocessing.

claims.claim: From before to after the experiment, the overall simulator sickness increased significantly.
claims.source: From before (M ± SD: 8.68 ± 2.82, range: 6–17) to after the experiment (M ± SD: 11.82 ± 5.24, range: 6–29), the overall simulator sickness (e.g., nausea, headache) increased significantly (t(36) = 3.72, p = 0.0007).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the questionnaire data.

claims.claim: The retrospective emotional arousal ratings for the VR experience, averaged across all subjects and timepoints, were 46.94 ± 12.50 in the nomov condition.
claims.source: The retrospective emotional arousal ratings for the VR experience, averaged across all subjects and timepoints, were 46.94 ± 12.50 (M ± SD, range: 16.17–66.29) in the nomov and 50.06 ± 12.55 (M ± SD, range: 18.00–69.94) in the mov condition.
claims.evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the arousal ratings.

claims.claim: The retrospective emotional arousal ratings for the VR experience, averaged across all subjects and timepoints, were 50.06 ± 12.55 in the mov condition.

claims.evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the arousal ratings.

claims.claim: The emotional arousal was highest for the Andes Coaster, lower for the Space Coaster, and lowest for the break.
claims.source: Qualitatively, the emotional arousal was highest for the Andes Coaster, lower for the Space Coaster, and lowest for the break (see Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative observation supported by Figure 5.

claims.claim: For 24/26 (92.30%) participants in the nomov condition, the component with the highest absolute lambda value corresponded to the one that maximized the negative correlation between subjective ratings and alpha power.
claims.source: SPoC results showed that for 24/26 (92.30%) participants in the nomov and 16/19 (84.21%) participants in the mov condition (see Figure 10—source data 1 for single-participant results), the component with the highest absolute lambda value corresponded to the one that maximized the negative correlation between z (normalized and mean-centred subjective ratings) and alpha power.

claims.claim: For 16/19 (84.21%) participants in the mov condition, the component with the highest absolute lambda value corresponded to the one that maximized the negative correlation between subjective ratings and alpha power.

claims.evidence: This is a result from the SPoC analysis.

claims.claim: Based on permutation-based testing, the negative correlation was statistically significant (p < 0.05) in 8/26 (30.76%) participants for the nomov condition.
claims.source: Based on permutation-based testing (1000 iterations; exact p values are reported in Figure 10—source data 1), the negative correlation was statistically significant (p < 0.05) in 8/26 (30.76%) participants for the nomov and 7/19 (36.84%) participants for the mov condition.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the SPoC analysis.

claims.claim: Based on permutation-based testing, the negative correlation was statistically significant (p < 0.05) in 7/19 (36.84%) participants for the mov condition.
claims.source: Based on permutation-based testing (1000 iterations; exact p values are reported in Figure 10—source data 1), the negative correlation was statistically significant (p < 0.05) in 8/26 (30.76%) participants for the nomov and 7/19 (36.84%) participants for the mov condition.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the SPoC analysis.

claims.claim: The mean Pearson correlation value between the target variable z and zest was significantly lower than the average of single participants' permuted ones for both the nomov and the mov condition.
claims.source: The mean Pearson correlation value between the target variable z and zest (estimated target variable) was significantly lower than the average of single participants' permuted ones for both the nomov (M ± SD: –0.25 ± 0.12; range: –0.53 to + 0.09; tnomov(25) = –3.62; p < 0.01) and the mov condition (M ± SD: –0.25 ± 0.12; range: –0.52 to +0.04; tmov(18) = –3.13; p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the SPoC analysis.

claims.claim: The classifier based on CSP was able to decode significantly above chance level whether a subject experienced high or low emotional arousal during a given second of the experience.
claims.source: The classifier based on CSP was able to decode significantly above chance level whether a subject experienced high or low emotional arousal during a given second of the experience.
claims.evidence: This is a main result from the CSP analysis.

claims.claim: On average, the classification accuracy was 60.83% ± 7.40% for the nomov condition.
claims.source: On average, the classification accuracy was 60.83% ± 7.40% (M ± SD; range: 47.22–77.78%) for the nomov, and 60.76% ± 6.58% (M ± SD; range: 48.33–71.67%) for the mov condition.

claims.claim: On average, the classification accuracy was 60.76% ± 6.58% for the mov condition.

claims.claim: Both nomov and mov classification accuracies were significantly above chance level.

claims.claim: At the single-subject level, the classification accuracy was significantly above chance level (p < 0.05) for 17/26 (65.38%) participants in the nomov condition.
claims.source: At the single-subject level, the classification accuracy was significantly above chance level (p < 0.05) for 17/26 (65.38%) participants in the nomov, and for 12/19 (63.16%) participants in the mov condition (see Figure 10—source data 1 for single-participant results).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the CSP analysis.

claims.claim: At the single-subject level, the classification accuracy was significantly above chance level (p < 0.05) for 12/19 (63.16%) participants in the mov condition.
claims.source: At the single-subject level, the classification accuracy was significantly above chance level (p < 0.05) for 17/26 (65.38%) participants in the nomov, and for 12/19 (63.16%) participants in the mov condition (see Figure 10—source data 1 for single-participant results).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the CSP analysis.

claims.claim: Under sub-blocked chronological cross-validation and block permutation evaluation, the average decoding performance (ROC-AUC) for CSP was significantly above chance level in both the nomov and mov conditions.
claims.source: Also under these – more strict – evaluation criteria, the average decoding performance (ROC-AUC) for CSP was significantly above chance level, both in the nomov (ROC-AUC: 0.61 ± 0.09 M ± SD, range: 0.42–0.79; t(25) = 4.59, p < 0.001) and in the mov condition (ROC-AUC: 0.60 ± 0.09 M ± SD, range: 0.44–0.74; t(18) = 3.27, p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the control analysis with stricter evaluation criteria.

claims.claim: On the single-subject level with permutation tests, decoding performance was significantly (p < 0.05) higher when decoding the actual, unpermuted labels compared to the block-permuted labels for 9/26 (34.62%) participants in the nomov condition.
claims.source: On the single-subject level (as assessed by permutation tests), decoding performance was significantly (p < 0.05) higher when decoding the actual, unpermuted labels compared to the block-permuted labels for 9/26 (34.62%) participants in the nomov and 5/19 (26.32%) participants in the mov condition.

claims.claim: On the single-subject level with permutation tests, decoding performance was significantly (p < 0.05) higher when decoding the actual, unpermuted labels compared to the block-permuted labels for 5/19 (26.32%) participants in the mov condition.

claims.evidence: This is a result from the control analysis with permutation testing.

claims.claim: The mean classification accuracy for LSTM was 59.42% ± 4.57% for the nomov condition.

claims.claim: The mean classification accuracy for LSTM was 61.29% ± 4.5% for the mov condition.

claims.claim: Both nomov and mov LSTM classification accuracies were significantly above chance level.

claims.claim: At the single-subject level, the LSTM classification accuracy was significantly above chance level for 16/26 (61.54%) participants in the nomov condition.

claims.claim: At the single-subject level, the LSTM classification accuracy was significantly above chance level for 16/19 (84.21%) participants in the mov condition.

claims.evidence: This is a result from the LSTM analysis.

claims.claim: The correlation between the two binary classification approaches (CSP, LSTM) was significant, irrespective of the experimental condition.
claims.source: The (positive) correlation between the two binary classification approaches (CSP, LSTM) was significant (after Bonferroni multiple-comparison correction), irrespective of the experimental condition (nomov, mov), meaning that subjects who could be better classified with CSP also yielded better results in the LSTM-based classification.
claims.evidence: This is a result comparing the two classification methods.

claims.claim: In a repeated-measures ANOVA testing for differences in the accuracies of the two binary classification models (CSP, LSTM) and the two conditions (nomov, mov), none of the effects was significant.
claims.source: In a repeated-measures ANOVA testing for differences in the accuracies of the two binary classification models (CSP, LSTM) and the two conditions (nomov, mov), none of the effects was significant: neither the main effect model (F(1,17) = 0.02, p = 0.904) nor the main effect condition (F(1,17) = 0.72, p = 0.408) or their interaction (F(1,17) = 1.59, p = 0.225).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing models and conditions.

claims.claim: SPoC and CSP performed significantly above chance level also when trained and tested on data without the break section.

claims.evidence: This is a result from the control analysis excluding the break.

claims.source: For CSP on data without the break, the average classification performance (ROC-AUC) was 0.57 ± 0.10 (M ± SD; range: 0.28–0.78) in the nomov and 0.59 ± 0.09 (M ± SD; range: 0.45–0.77) in the mov condition (see previous paragraph for the decoding performance with the break included).

claims.evidence: This is a result from the control analysis excluding the break.

claims.claim: Average CSP model performances without the break were still significantly above chance level in both movement conditions.
claims.source: Average model performances were still significantly above chance level (means of the block permutation distributions on the single-subject level) in both movement conditions (nomov: t(25) = 2.89, p < 0.01; mov: t(18) = 3.50, p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the control analysis excluding the break.

claims.claim: For SPoC on data without the break, the average Pearson correlation between z and zest was significantly smaller (more negative) than the average of single participants' permuted correlation values for both the nomov and the mov condition.

claims.evidence: This is a result from the control analysis excluding the break.

claims.source: Removing the break from the training data overall numerically decreased the decoding performances of both models.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the control analysis.

claims.claim: For CSP, the decrease in performance after removing the break was significant in the nomov condition but not significant in the mov condition.
claims.source: For CSP, the decrease was significant in the nomov (t(25) = 2.23, p = 0.034) and not significant in the mov condition (t(18) = 0.57, p = 0.58).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the control analysis.

claims.claim: For SPoC, the decrease in performance after removing the break was not significant in both conditions.
claims.source: For SPoC, the decrease (Pearson correlation) was not significant in both conditions (nomov: t(25) = –1.66, p = 0.108; mov: t(18) = –1.13, p = 0.269).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the control analysis.

claims.claim: The findings support previous results from classical studies and confirm them under more naturalistic conditions.
claims.source: In addition to extending our knowledge about the functional anatomy of emotional arousal, these findings support previous results from classical studies and confirm them under more naturalistic conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's contribution.

claims.claim: The results provide evidence that the neural mechanisms reflected in modulations of alpha power bear information about the subjective emotional state of a person undergoing an immersive and emotionally arousing experience.
claims.source: Our results provide evidence that the neural mechanisms reflected in modulations of alpha power – particularly in parieto-occipital regions – also bear information about the subjective emotional state of a person undergoing an immersive and emotionally arousing experience.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claims.claim: The study suggests that findings from event-related, simplified stimulation generalize to more naturalistic settings.
claims.source: Our study thus suggests that findings from event-related, simplified stimulation generalize to more naturalistic (i.e., dynamic and interactive) settings.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claims.claim: Modulations of alpha power were linked to attention and memory.
claims.source: Paralleling the idea of emotional arousal being a dimension of 'core affect' (Russell and Barrett, 1999) and a psychological primitive that underlies many mental phenomena, also alpha oscillations have been connected to various psychological 'core processes': for instance, modulations of alpha power were linked to attention (Van Diepen et al., 2019) and memory (Klimesch, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Van Diepen et al., 2019 and Klimesch, 2012.

claims.claim: Modulations of alpha oscillations over parietal sensors have been linked to threat processing.
claims.source: In line with this, modulations of alpha oscillations over parietal sensors have been linked to threat processing (Grimshaw et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Grimshaw et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The inverse modelling localized arousal-related alpha sources in sensorimotor cortices, which could correspond to somatic experiences typically associated with rollercoasters.
claims.source: Moreover, our inverse modelling (Figure 9) has also localized arousal-related alpha sources in sensorimotor cortices, which could correspond to somatic experiences typically associated with rollercoasters.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the source localization results shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Lateralization of alpha power has been observed in working-memory and resting-state studies.
claims.source: However, it is unclear to which extent these effects are specific to arousal, as lateralization of alpha power has also been observed in working-memory (Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2020) and resting-state studies (Ocklenburg et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2020 and Ocklenburg et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Despite the incongruence between VR rollercoaster-induced visual stimulation and vestibular signals, only one participant stopped the experiment because of cybersickness.
claims.source: Despite the incongruence between VR rollercoaster-induced visual stimulation and vestibular signals, which may lead to motion sickness (Reason and Brand, 1975), only one of our participants stopped the experiment because of cybersickness.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claims.claim: Shorter exposure times and experiences that elicit stronger feelings of presence have been associated with lower levels of cybersickness.
claims.source: Shorter exposure times (Rebenitsch and Owen, 2016) and experiences that elicit stronger feelings of presence have been associated with lower levels of cybersickness (Weech et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Rebenitsch and Owen, 2016 and Weech et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The performance of all three decoding models did not differ significantly for both conditions (nomov, mov).
claims.source: Ultimately, the performance of all three decoding models did not differ significantly for both conditions (nomov, mov).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the comparison of model performances.

claims.claim: With appropriate quality assurance during data acquisition and analysis, EEG can be combined with immersive VR and free head movements.
claims.source: We suggest that, with appropriate quality assurance during data acquisition and analysis (leading to more data rejection/correction for mov than for nomov), EEG can be combined with immersive VR and free head movements.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claims.claim: The normalized and averaged SPoC topoplots and source localizations in both conditions resemble the ones extracted via CSP to maximize power for the low-arousal epochs.
claims.source: The similarity between the two approaches (SPoC, CSP) and their interpretability becomes apparent in the resulting spatial patterns: the normalized and averaged SPoC topoplots and source localizations in both conditions (nomov, mov) resemble the ones extracted via CSP to maximize power for the low-arousal epochs of the experience (Figures 6 and 9).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing the spatial patterns shown in Figures 6 and 9.

claims.claim: SPoC and CSP exploited similar spatial informational patterns in the input data.
claims.source: This indicates that SPoC and CSP exploited similar spatial informational patterns in the input data.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of spatial patterns.

claims.claim: The LSTM can extract features from neural input components that reflect changes in subjective emotional arousal.
claims.source: We found that the LSTM can extract features from neural input components that reflect changes in subjective emotional arousal and that the accuracy of its predictions in both conditions (nomov, mov) matched closely the ones of CSP (see Figures 8 and 10).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the LSTM analysis.

claims.claim: The accuracy of LSTM predictions in both conditions matched closely the ones of CSP.
claims.source: We found that the LSTM can extract features from neural input components that reflect changes in subjective emotional arousal and that the accuracy of its predictions in both conditions (nomov, mov) matched closely the ones of CSP (see Figures 8 and 10).

claims.claim: The strong correlation between the predictions of the two models (CSP and LSTM) suggests that the LSTM extracts similar information as the CSP to make its prediction, namely power.

claims.claim: The LSTM model converged in less than 200 training iterations on a relatively small dataset.
claims.source: Although it is often stated that deep learning models require large datasets (for an empirical perspective, see Hestness et al., 2017), our model, with its architecture of one to two LSTM layers followed by one to two fully connected layers, converged in less than 200 training iterations on a relatively small dataset.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the LSTM training.

claims.claim: The quick convergence of the LSTM is partly due to the fast gradient flow through the memory cell during the weight update.
claims.source: This quick convergence is partly due to the fast gradient flow through the memory cell of the LSTM during the weight update, which is an additional advantage of the LSTM over other RNNs (Doetsch et al., 2014; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Doetsch et al., 2014 and Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997.

claims.claim: SPoC, CSP, and LSTM can be used to decode subjective emotional arousal from EEG acquired during a naturalistic immersive VR experience.

claims.claim: The relatively low accuracy may be a consequence of the fast-changing events in the VR experience, the asynchronicity of the two data streams, the high inter-individual variability in the interpretability of subjective self-reports, and the 'single-trial' study design.
claims.source: This may be a consequence of (1) the fast-changing events in the VR experience (particularly the rollercoasters), (2) the asynchronicity of the two data streams as participants retrieved their emotional states from memory in retrospective ratings, (3) the generally high inter-individual variability in the interpretability of subjective self-reports (Blascovich, 1990), and (4) the 'single-trial' study design and its relatively short time series.

results.result: The study successfully combined immersive VR with EEG recording in 37 participants who experienced two rollercoaster rides while EEG was recorded, then retrospectively rated their emotional arousal. The experimental setup included both head-movement and no-head-movement conditions, with appropriate counterbalancing and quality control measures.
results.evaluation: The experimental design is well-documented with clear sample sizes (C2, C50, C51), appropriate exclusion criteria (C49), counterbalancing (C48), and detailed technical specifications (C39-C42). The arousal ratings show expected patterns with highest arousal for Andes coaster (C55), and simulator sickness was monitored (C52). The methodological rigor supports the feasibility of combining VR with EEG.

results.result: SPoC analysis revealed a significant negative correlation between parieto-occipital alpha power and subjective emotional arousal ratings. For the majority of participants (92% nomov, 84% mov), the component with highest lambda value maximized the negative correlation, with group-level significance (p < 0.01) and mean correlations of -0.25 in both conditions.
results.evaluation: While group-level statistics are significant (C60), only 30-37% of individual participants showed significant correlations after permutation testing (C58, C59). The modest effect sizes (r = -0.25) and low single-subject significance rates raise questions about the robustness and generalizability of the finding. The result may be driven by a subset of participants or specific task features (e.g., the break period).

results.result: CSP-based classification successfully decoded high versus low emotional arousal states with mean accuracies of ~61% (significantly above chance) in both movement conditions. Under stricter sub-blocked cross-validation with permutation testing, performance remained significant at the group level (ROC-AUC ~0.60), though fewer individual participants showed significant effects.
results.evaluation: The CSP results show consistent above-chance classification with appropriate statistical testing including permutation controls (C67-C69). The convergence of results across standard and strict validation approaches strengthens confidence. However, the modest accuracy (~61%) and reduced single-subject significance under stricter testing (26-35% of participants, C68-C69) indicates the effect is real but moderate in strength.

results.result: LSTM-based classification achieved mean accuracies of 59-61% (significantly above chance, p < 0.001) for decoding emotional arousal states, with notably higher single-subject significance rates in the movement condition (84% of participants) compared to no-movement (62%).
results.evaluation: The LSTM results are statistically significant at the group level (C72) with comparable performance to CSP. The higher single-subject significance rate in the movement condition (C74) is interesting but unexplained. The lack of permutation testing for LSTM (acknowledged by authors) is a limitation, though the convergence with CSP results provides some validation.

results.result: The three decoding approaches (SPoC, CSP, LSTM) showed convergent results with significant correlations between CSP and LSTM predictions, similar spatial patterns between SPoC and CSP, and no significant differences in performance between models or movement conditions.
results.evaluation: The convergence across methods (C75, C96, C99) strengthens confidence in the findings. The similar spatial patterns (C96) and lack of performance differences (C76, C94) suggest the methods are capturing the same underlying signal. The inference that LSTM extracts similar power-based features as CSP (C100) is reasonable given the strong correlation.

results.result: Control analyses excluding the break period showed that both SPoC and CSP remained significantly above chance at the group level, though with numerically decreased performance. The decrease was significant for CSP in the no-movement condition but not in the movement condition.
results.evaluation: The control analysis appropriately tests whether results depend on the distinctive break period. Both methods remain significant without the break (C77, C80, C81), indicating the effect is not solely driven by this contrast. The performance decrease (C82-C84) is expected given less training data and narrower arousal range, and the pattern of results (significant decrease only in nomov for CSP) suggests some condition-specific effects.

results.result: Source localization using eLORETA identified parieto-occipital regions as the primary sources of arousal-related alpha oscillations, with additional contributions from sensorimotor cortices potentially corresponding to somatic experiences during the rollercoaster rides.
results.evaluation: The source localization results (C105, C90) are consistent with prior literature on alpha oscillations and emotional arousal. The identification of parieto-occipital sources aligns with the scalp topographies and the hypothesis. The interpretation of sensorimotor contributions (C90) is speculative but reasonable given the rollercoaster context.

results.result: The study demonstrates that EEG can be successfully combined with immersive VR and head movements with appropriate quality control, though the decoding accuracy was relatively modest (~60%) compared to other EEG paradigms, likely due to the naturalistic, dynamic stimulation and retrospective rating approach.
results.evaluation: The feasibility conclusion (C95) is supported by the successful data collection and comparable results across movement conditions. The acknowledgment of modest accuracy (C106) and discussion of contributing factors (C107-C110) shows appropriate self-criticism. The retrospective rating approach (C109, C110) was designed to minimize biases, though some asynchronicity between experience and rating is unavoidable.

results.result: The study confirms that findings from event-related, simplified stimulation regarding the relationship between alpha power and emotional arousal generalize to more naturalistic, dynamic VR settings, demonstrating that subjective emotional arousal can be decoded from neural information in naturalistic research designs.
results.evaluation: The main conclusions (C86, C87, C120) are supported by the convergent results across multiple analytical approaches. The claim of generalization from lab to naturalistic settings (C85, C87, C119) is justified given the successful replication of the alpha-arousal relationship in a more complex, dynamic context. However, the modest effect sizes and individual variability suggest the generalization is not perfect.

results.result: The LSTM model converged rapidly (< 200 iterations) on the relatively small dataset, likely due to efficient gradient flow through LSTM memory cells and the spatial-spectral filtering preprocessing that extracted narrow-band alpha components.
results.evaluation: The observation of rapid convergence (C101) is documented, and the explanations involving LSTM architecture (C102) and preprocessing (C103) are reasonable and supported by citations. This demonstrates the practical applicability of deep learning to sparse neuroscience datasets when appropriate preprocessing is applied.

results.result: The study has limitations including use of commercial VR content without source code access, relatively short recording times leading to data sparsity, and the inherent challenges of decoding from sparse naturalistic data, though cross-validation was used to mitigate limited data issues.
results.evaluation: The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations regarding stimulus control (C113, C114), data sparsity (C115, C116), and analytical approaches (C117). These are genuine limitations that affect interpretability and generalizability. The acknowledgment that more data would improve robustness (C118) is a standard limitation in machine learning studies.

results.result: Immersive VR enables naturalistic neuroscientific studies while maintaining experimental control, and combining VR with neuroimaging may increase the generalizability and real-world relevance of neuroscientific findings by allowing study of the brain under conditions it was optimized for.
results.evaluation: These claims represent the broader motivation and implications of the work. The successful execution of the study (C1) supports the feasibility claim. The arguments about naturalistic experiments (C27, C28) are well-supported by citations and the study's results. The forward-looking statement (C121) is appropriately framed as aspirational rather than demonstrated.
